newsitem.title: UK: EU pact hopes keep dollar underpinned in Europe.
newsitem.headline: EU pact hopes keep dollar underpinned in Europe.

text.p: The dollar tiptoed lower against the mark by European midsession, but traders blamed mild profit-taking and said sentiment remained healthy as players banked on a deal on the EU stability pact at the Amsterdam summit.

Though accord on the pact -- which aims to enforce budgetary rigour after EMU begins -- is now largely priced in, analysts said it would support the dollar by fuelling fears that the mark would be swallowed up into a weak single currency.
By contrast, dollar/yen came under some pressure as the market awaited this week's U.S. and Japan trade data ahead of the G7 summit in Denver, Colorado on June 20-22.
Figures out Tuesday are expected to show Japan's trade surplus grew in May, while April U.S. data out Thursday are forecast to reveal the opposite -- a widening trade deficit.

The market fears that the trade situation could prompt a clash between the U.S. and Japan in Denver, although an international monetary source helped calm those concerns today by saying G7 leaders may not single out Japan's surplus.
"The Japanese are hoping the trade number won't be a very poor one, and the U.S. the same, or there'll be increased criticism when they meet," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston in London.
The dollar slipped to 114.05/15 yen and 1.7336/43 marks by 1034 GMT from late Friday's European levels of 114.65/75 and 1.7365/75.
Mark/yen pointed up the contrasting forces at work on the dollar, falling to 65.77 from 65.99/02 late on Friday.

Upbeat comments from officials in Amsterdam nourished hopes of a deal on the stability pact, as the market waited to see exactly how EU leaders would address French demands for initiatives on jobs and greater economic policy coordination.
France last week sparked fears of EMU delay -- and a flight into marks -- when it asked for more time to study the pact.
"All eyes are on Amsterdam - that's going to overshadow any data from the U.S. for the next couple of days," said Elizabeth Cheale, trader at Dresdner Bank in London.

Still, U.S. data will continue to interest the market as it seeks clues to whether the Federal Reserve will hike rates when it next meets on July 1-2. Tuesday sees the release of May consumer prices, seen up an average 0.2 percent month-on-month.

"Most people are anticipating tomorrow's inflation figures are going to be fairly benign, and expectations about the next FOMC are definitely shifting into the camp of no policy move," said Stephen Hannah, direction of research at IBJ International.

Data out last Friday showed U.S. producer prices dropped 0.3 percent in May. That confounded market forecasts of a mild rise, and touched off a sharp rally in U.S. stocks and bonds as investors scaled back expectations of Fed tightening.
The asset rally benefited the dollar -- even though rate rises are traditionally viewed as currency-positive -- and analysts said the same scenario should unfold if the CPI numbers were subdued.
